name: North Side School House
aka: the first house built for a school in Chicago

documented_range.note: THE YEAR IS ATTESTED, THE MONTH IS NOT, AND THE BUILDING ITSELF IS DISPUTED BY THE MAN WHO TAUGHT IN IT. Andreas: 'It is stated in Mr. Wells's report that these gentlemen [Colonels Hamilton and Owen] afterwards built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Mr. Watkins continued his school, and that it was the first house built for a school in Chicago. BUT THIS DOES NOT RECUR TO MR. WATKINS'S RECOLLECTION.' Andreas prints the doubt and then, forty pages later, states the building as fact and dates it: 'John Watkins was then teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen, as has already been stated, in 1833.' A THIRD PASSAGE CORROBORATES A SCHOOL BUILDING THERE, independently of Wells: Andreas's Methodist chapter has Jesse Walker's first quarterly meeting held 'in the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle'. So a Watkins school-house existed on North Water Street near Clark in 1834, whatever Watkins remembered about who built it. The range opens on 1 January 1833 as the earliest day the attested year allows and closes at the end of 1835 as this record's claim horizon; no source follows the building past Watkins, who 'taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known'.

position.symbolic_location: North side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, on the North Water Street frontage.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND ONE BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT WHICH SIDE OF CLARK STREET IT WAS ON. The schools chapter says twice that the building stood 'on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street' and 'on the river bank just east of Clark Street'. The Methodist chapter says 'the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle' — which is WEST of Clark, about a block away. THE SCHOOLS CHAPTER IS ADOPTED because it is the more specific statement, it is made twice, and it is the chapter about this building; the church chapter is naming a meeting place in passing. IF THE CHURCH CHAPTER IS RIGHT, THIS BUILDING STANDS ABOUT 110 M WEST OF WHERE IT IS DRAWN. Method: Clark Street's modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447646.20, N 4637668.88, local E +573.5, N +273.1) and carried south on the OSM bearing, giving an east kerb 12.2 m east of it, half an 80 ft platted street; the 1834 north bank and the North Water Street frontage were read off the Wright 1834 sheet through this project's fitted affine, which puts the drawn bank at local N +98 along this stretch and the block row's south line — the street's north kerb — at about N +128. The building is set with its west face 6 m east of the Clark kerb and its south face 12.5 m north of the bank, i.e. on the bank strip the street occupies, which is what 'on the river bank' says. Facade bearing 180, due south to the river, is inferred from that frontage and from nothing anybody wrote. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus the ~5 m of reading the sheet by eye, plus the block-scale disagreement above, which is far larger than either. There is no modelled terrain under this building — it stands about 280 m east of the terrain box.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING. 7.3 x 5.5 m is 24 x 18 ft: a one-room schoolhouse large enough for the thirty scholars Watkins's subscription was written for. Every number is invented. BEWARE THE ONE DIMENSION THE SOURCE DOES GIVE, BECAUSE IT BELONGS TO A DIFFERENT BUILDING: Watkins's FIRST schoolroom, in the autumn of 1832, was Colonel Hamilton's horse stable — 'The building belonged to Colonel Hamilton, was erected for a horse stable and had been used as such. It was twelve feet square.' That is not this house, and a 12 ft square building is not what the second passage means by 'the first house built for a school in Chicago'.

construction.note: NOT ATTESTED, AND THE EVIDENCE POINTS BOTH WAYS AT THIS DATE. For log: everything standing on the north bank in the 1820s was log — Andreas, of 1823, 'All these houses were of logs' — and Wau-Bun's 1831 north bank is a ring of log buildings. Against it: 1833 is the year the town began building in frame, and the nearest comparable building we can date is frame — the Methodist meeting house put up at the corner of North Water and Clark Streets, one block away, on a contract signed 30 June 1834, 'a frame building twenty-six by thirty-eight feet; twelve-foot posts; sheeted and shingled roof'. A subscription schoolhouse built by two colonels in 1833 could be either. Log is recorded because it keeps this building with the older north-bank fabric it stood among, and it is tagged conjectural because that is a preference between two readings and not a derivation from evidence. THE CHOICE ALSO CHOSE THE ARCHETYPE: `log_dwelling` builds log by definition, so a frame reading would change the record's kind.

stories.note: Not attested. A one-room subscription school of 1833 is a single-storey building by type, and nothing in the accounts of Watkins's schools suggests otherwise.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft — one storey of wall plus a sill, the figure this project uses for its other single-storey log buildings. Compare the Methodist meeting house's contracted 'twelve-foot posts' a block away, which is a different and taller building and is why this number is inference rather than borrowed.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for a building of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One is the minimum for a schoolroom kept through Chicago winters and the normal number for a single-pen building. The COUNT is the inference; where the stack stands and what it is made of are the archetype's — docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

phases.change_note: The house Colonels Hamilton and Owen are said to have built for a school in 1833 on the north bank just east of Clark Street, in which John Watkins carried on the school he had begun in 1832 in Hamilton's twelve-foot horse stable. Its passage from subscription school to public school is a change of USE and does not open a new phase.

function.note: THE 1835 USE IS ATTESTED, WHICH IS NOT WHAT THIS RECORD EXPECTED TO FIND. Andreas's schools narrative, having just placed George Davis in the Presbyterian church 'later, in 1835', continues: 'John Watkins was THEN teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen.' So the building was in use as a public school in the year of the scene. THE GRAIN IS THE YEAR AND NOT THE DAY, and Andreas adds the limit himself: 'Mr. Watkins taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known.' A building may stand while its function lapses; here the function is attested for 1835 and cannot be tied to 1 July.

research_note: THE TOWN'S FIRST PURPOSE-BUILT SCHOOLHOUSE, IF IT WAS BUILT: Andreas carries the claim from Mr. Wells's report and prints, in the same breath, that John Watkins did not recollect it — then states it as fact forty pages later when he needs it to place the 1835 public school. This record follows Andreas's second statement and keeps his first as the doubt it is. TWO THINGS THE PROJECT'S DOSSIER DID NOT HAVE, both from Andreas at full text: the Watkins letter to the Calumet Club of 22 June 1879, which describes his first school as Hamilton's twelve-foot-square horse stable 'about half way between the lake and the forks of the river' and is the reason that dimension must not be attached to this building; and the Methodist chapter's competing location for 'the Watkins school-house', on North Water Street BETWEEN CLARK AND LASALLE, which is the other side of Clark from the schools chapter's 'just east of Clark Street'. THE SAME PASSAGE CARRIES A THIRD FINDING THIS PARCEL DID NOT BUILD: the first Methodist meeting house was erected 'at the corner of North Water and Clark streets' on a contract signed 30 June 1834 for 'a frame building twenty-six by thirty-eight feet; twelve-foot posts; sheeted and shingled roof; a neat pulpit', finished and in use to 1836. That is a documented, dimensioned north-bank building standing on the scene date, it is NOT this project's walker_meeting_house, and it is not yet in the dataset. See docs/RESEARCH/north_side_school_1833.md.
